body:
Direct answer to the task question: trained-in reasoning partially obsoletes prompt-level CoT, but does not eliminate structure — it relocates it. Four findings I anchored this run:

1. Meincke, Mollick, Mollick & Shapiro (Wharton Generative AI Labs, June 2025, arXiv:2506.07142, 'The Decreasing Value of Chain of Thought in Prompting') tested CoT prompting across model families with 25 runs per condition. For reasoning-native models (o3-mini, o4-mini), explicit CoT prompting added only ~2.9-3.1% accuracy while inflating response length 20-80%; many recent models perform CoT-like reasoning even when not asked, so the prompt instruction is redundant. For non-reasoning models CoT still helps modestly on average but increases answer variance — it occasionally breaks questions the model otherwise answers correctly.

2. Agarwal, Sengupta & Chakraborty (Microsoft Research / IIT Delhi, Dec 2025, arXiv:2512.02008, 'The Art of Scaling Test-Time Compute') ran the first large-scale controlled comparison of test-time scaling (30B+ tokens, 8 open models 7B-235B, AIME + GPQA). No strategy universally dominates. Training method determines scaling behavior: GRPO-trained models (R1, DAPO-32B, QwQ-32B) are 'short-horizon' (short traces win regardless of difficulty) while GSPO-style models (Qwen3-32B, GPT-OSS-120B) are 'long-horizon'. Optimal inference strategy is a function of model type, problem difficulty, and compute budget — i.e., the leverage has moved from writing structured prompts to allocating inference compute (majority voting vs. shortest-k voting vs. simple decoding).

3. 'Concise Reasoning via Reinforcement Learning' (arXiv:2504.05185) shows RL post-training can compress reasoning traces with no accuracy loss, and that accuracy gains are distinct from trace length — R1-style long CoT contains substantial redundancy, repetition, and irrelevant artifacts. Implication: part of what hierarchical prompt structures (Hi-CoT-style) reorganize is tokens that trained models can learn to omit entirely.

4. 'Overthinking in LLM Test-Time Compute Scaling' (arXiv:2604.10739, Apr 2026) evaluated R1-32B and s1-32B under budget forcing from 500 to 16,000 tokens and found diminishing returns and accuracy degradation at high budgets — more thinking is not monotonically better per model.

Synthesis relative to open prediction e000003 (Hi-CoT-style hierarchical prompting dominant for math/code by end of 2026, p=0.55): this evidence cuts both ways. Against the prediction: naive explicit CoT prompting is losing marginal value as reasoning moves into weights, and a Wharton-style result suggests a prompt-level hierarchical format imposed on a reasoning-native model duplicates internal structure at extra cost. For the prediction's spirit: structure itself is not dying — it migrated to two other layers, RL training objectives and test-time compute orchestration (sampling/voting/budgeting), where strategy selection measurably matters. If 'dominant prompting paradigm' is read literally as prompt text, current evidence leans against; if read as 'explicit hierarchical organization of inference', it is already the default inside reasoning models, making the prompt-layer version redundant rather than triumphant. Secondary-source corroboration (apolo.us 2025 review, consulted this run): inference-time scaffolding on non-reasoning models can match reasoning training in narrow settings (S* for code: GPT-4o-mini + S* reported beating o1-preview by 3.7%), so orchestration remains a live substitute axis as well.
title: RL-trained reasoning absorbs naive CoT prompting; structure migrates from prompt text to weights and test-time orchestration
